Deltarune Chapter 6 'Structurally Complete,' Chapter 7 Development Underway

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that chapter 5 of Toby Fox’s newest indie game opus, Deltarune, rolled out back in June of this year.
  • Based on some little hints that Fox has previously dropped, Chapter 6 will be when the game starts reaching its narrative crux, bringing an end to “wacky silly adventures” in the face of all the mysteries that have been building up, and there are a lot of them.
  • In a recent development, in the newest edition of the Deltarune newsletter for Fall 2026, Fox unveiled that Chapter 6 is “structurally complete,” in that you can technically play it from start to finish.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that chapter 5 of Toby Fox’s newest indie game opus, Deltarune, rolled out back in June of this year. It’s kind of interesting to think about; when that chapter launched, it completely dominated the gaming sphere for a good month, even if it didn’t quite hit with everyone. Now that GTA 6 is out and completely taken over the scene, it’s gone largely quiet outside of its specific fanbase. Still, perhaps that’s for the best. A little less attention means that Fox and his team will have some extra breathing room as they work on the next stretch of the game, which is set to encompass both Chapter 6 and Chapter 7.

Based on some little hints that Fox has previously dropped, Chapter 6 will be when the game starts reaching its narrative crux, bringing an end to “wacky silly adventures” in the face of all the mysteries that have been building up, and there are a lot of them. It’s still going to be a while before we actually get to see any of this, mind you, but according to Fox, development is going pretty swimmingly.

In a recent development, in the newest edition of the Deltarune newsletter for Fall 2026, Fox unveiled that Chapter 6 is “structurally complete,” in that you can technically play it from start to finish. The next orders of business will be to hammer out the nitty-gritty details, as well as get things rolling in earnest on Chapter 7.

Industry observers note that as Fox explained in the newsletter, Chapter 6 is a “structurally complete draft that can be played from the beginning to the end. All the maps, events, and battles exist,” though he parenthetically noted that there’s a particular optional event that’s causing the overall development to drag out a bit.

Recent findings suggest that “By the time you read this, we should have started the localization and some preliminary testing. Much of the game looks complete… but, some important scenes and details are still undercooked in their presentation, so it's going to take a bit longer before we can really move to full-on testing,” Fox stated.

He admitted that, while Chapter 6 will be shorter in length than the previous chapters, it’s going to be a pivotal one, and he wants it to hit as hard as it possibly can. In short, this is not a process that can be rushed; it’ll only be ready once he’s satisfied with it.

By the time you read this, we should have started the localization and some preliminary testing.

On the bright side, thanks to a fan vote, Fox opted to share a brief sneak peek of Chapter 6 in the form of a quote unquote “stupid scene” involving Queen meeting with Pink in Castle Town and being… her Queenly self, let’s say. Hey, it made me laugh.

The newsletter also shared an update on Chapter 7, though as Fox rather succinctly puts it, “Well, we've only just started…”.

While development on Chapter 7 has only just begun, Fox feels as though he’s on the right track with his team and their work. Apparently, the way they’re handling development is by having Fox read out the events and dialogue of the chapter to the team, then stopping just as the story reaches a critical point. The only way for the team to find out what happens next is for more of the game to be completed. A bit of an unusual approach, but apparently, “Everyone agrees it's more fun this way.”.

With so much of Deltarune already under the team’s belt, Fox is feeling optimistic as they all get started in earnest on Chapter 7. “Unlike every other Chapter, I actually feel like I know what I'm doing this time, so I have a lot of confidence...!”.

Fox concluded the newsletter with a reminder that, as development on the game goes on, the dev team keeps getting bigger, which is why more time is needed to ensure everything comes out right.

“I know it's probably annoying to not have any updates, but no news is good news.”.

In a statement posted yesterday, Killing Floor developers Tripwire Interactive have declared that the studio is laying off 36 "talented" internal staff as part of a "workforce reduction". The job cuts come 16 months after the release of Killing Floor 3 (which James didn't care for), and within hours of unrelated yet equally dispiriting redunancies at Skydance Games.

Tripwire's announcement claims that this was "not an easy decision, but unfortunately a necessary one for the organisation," adding that "these are truly great people who are exceptional at their roles, and we will help support these individuals with compassion and dignity during this transition." There's a small hope in me that this might mean helping those affected find new jobs promptly, though it's hard to stay optimistic when mass layoffs in games development have become such a regular occurrence.

Despite this post primarily being about the loss of 36 livelihoods, Tripwire are quick to reassure fans that Killing Floor 3's post-launch updates remain in active development, as does their comedy shark-action sequel Maneater 2. The studio "remain committed to our awesome community", they say; apparently just not to their awesome employees.

This news also arrives just days after Tripwire expanded its publishing business to support small indie developers, and less than a year after its last round of layoffs in March. Tripwire also happens to have been acquired by layoff extraordinaire corporation Embracer in 2022, just for some relevant context.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Volkswagen GTI badge has been a staple in automotive culture for 50 years, and it’s clearly not getting sidelined anytime soon. VW just released the ID.Polo GTI Clubsport concept, an electric track-focused GTI that slots in as the automaker’s fourth new GTI variant this year.

Recent findings suggest that while it’s not heading to production, the Clubsport concept is a peek into the possibilities riding on the electric ID.Polo GTI, which became the first EV to wear the GTI badge when it was released earlier this year. The standard ID.Polo GTI, which isn’t sold in the United States, reaches 62 mph in 6.8 seconds thanks to a 223-hp electric motor mounted to the front axle.

See all results for Volkswagen ID.GTI for sale near 60629.

In a recent development, the Clubsport concept ups the ante, with VW claiming it will hit 62 mph in just 4.7 seconds with the help of launch control and a more powerful APP550 electric motor. The upgraded motor, which is typically used to power the rear wheels of larger models like the ID.Tiguan and ID.7, sends 362 horsepower to the front wheels and nearly doubles the standard electric GTI’s torque output from 213 to 406 pound-feet.

According to recent reports, volkswagen also equipped the concept vehicle with an electronically regulated front differential lock, a performance-tuned adaptive suspension system, and ceramic brakes with a one-box brake setup. The high-performance powertrain fits into an equally aggressive two-door build, complete with a large front splitter, diffuser, and a flared rear wing.

Industry observers note that rather than the typical five-seater setup, the Clubsport concept houses two Recaro bucket seats with red five-point harnesses. A Tornado Red roll bar replaces the rear seats, and the cockpit is solely reserved for racing needs, meaning the standard infotainment system is also omitted. The cabin is finished in a dark microfiber material and trimmed with red stitching.

Volkswagen calls this concept the “perfect match of heritage and future,” and the automaker says its young employees were involved in much of the concept’s realization. The ID.Polo GTI Clubsport concept won’t ever make it to VW showrooms, but it’ll be displayed next week at the Essen Motor Show in Essen, Germany.

In a recent development, alayna Wilkening grew up reading motorsport magazines and following her grandpa around his Chevrolet dealership's showroom floor. In true Hoosier fashion, her first car was a hot pink custom cardboard "Fiero-vette" for her kindergarten Kindy 500 race. She now autocrosses a 1994 Miata with her dad, which she learned to drive the night before her first event. Alayna went to Indiana University and graduated with a degree in journalism and a minor in graphic design. As a testament to her great taste in cars, her first real one was a metallic orange 2007 Chevy HHR, which she lovingly called "The Dumptruck.".

#86576. Breaking: Scientists create a remarkable newly introduced rechargeable battery using vitamin B12

Breaking: Scientists create a remarkable newly introduced rechargeable battery using vitamin B12

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that scientists have found an unexpected new use for vitamin B12, a nutrient best known for its importance to human health.
  • Vitamin B12 is essential for normal bodily function and is naturally present in animal products.
  • Sources indicate that now, scientists are exploring an entirely different application.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that scientists have found an unexpected new use for vitamin B12, a nutrient best known for its importance to human health. Researchers at the University of Córdoba have incorporated the vitamin into a rechargeable battery, demonstrating for the first time that it can serve as a catalyst in this type of energy storage system.

Vitamin B12 is essential for normal bodily function and is naturally present in animal products. The vitamin is produced by certain bacteria, which occur in nature and are also grown commercially to supply the food and pharmaceutical industries. In addition to its established applications in medicine, nutrition, and veterinary care, B12 is used to address certain nutritional deficiencies. It has also become popular alongside other B vitamins as a hangover remedy because of its potential to help reduce fatigue.

Sources indicate that now, scientists are exploring an entirely different application. By using the vitamin to support the chemical reactions inside a battery, they have developed a prototype capable of completing up to 250 charging and discharging cycles.

How Vitamin B12 Makes a Rechargeable Battery Possible.

Sources indicate that the latest battery was developed by the Physical Chemistry research group (FQM-204) at the University of Córdoba's Chemical Institute for Energy and the Environment (IQUEMA). It uses zinc and oxygen from the surrounding air to produce electricity, with vitamin B12, also called cobalamin, playing a crucial role in the process.

Recent findings suggest that to make the design work, the researchers attached vitamin B12 molecules to single-walled carbon nanotubes. The vitamin contains cobalt (III) at its center, which helps drive the electrochemical reactions needed for the battery to function.

The team has previously experimented with natural molecules as battery catalysts, including hemoglobin and catalase. These substances contain iron (II) and iron (III), respectively. Vitamin B12 represents the group's third effort to use a biological molecule for this purpose, but it has delivered an vital advance: a battery that can be recharged repeatedly, completing as many as 250 cycles.

One of the biggest obstacles was keeping vitamin B12 inside the battery. Because the vitamin dissolves readily in water, it would normally be difficult to retain in a system that relies on a water-based electrolyte.

The researchers overcame this problem by securing the vitamin to carbon nanotubes, using an approach inspired by how amino acids connect to form proteins.

Manuel Cano Luna, one of the study's authors, explained that "we looked at the properties we can find in naturally occurring materials to use them in newly introduced batteries," while describing the team's search for useful biological compounds.

Their attachment technique imitates "the process by which amino acids bind together in proteins.".

Alongside Cano Luna, the research team included Valentín García Caballero, Miguel López León, Pablo Gómez Argudo, Luis Camacho Delgado, José Miguel Rodríguez Mellado, María Teresa Martín Romero, José Abad López, and Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero.

A Safer, Lighter Alternative to Lithium-Ion Batteries.

The findings, published in the Journal of Materials Chemistry A, could contribute to the development of battery technologies that depend less on the materials used in conventional lithium-ion batteries.

According to recent reports, although lithium-ion batteries are widely used, obtaining their raw materials can involve significant economic, environmental, and social challenges. Zinc-air batteries offer a potential alternative because they can store substantial amounts of energy relative to their weight while relying on materials that are more readily available.

Sources indicate that zinc is abundant and recyclable, and these batteries use oxygen from the surrounding atmosphere as part of their energy-producing reactions. Because they draw oxygen from the air rather than storing all the necessary reactants internally, they can also be lighter than other battery designs.

According to recent reports, this advantage has helped make zinc-air batteries increasingly useful in compact electronic devices, particularly hearing aids. Another benefit is their use of non-flammable, water-based electrolytes, which can reduce fire risks and improve safety.

Why Vitamin B12 Is Key to Recharging.

A major challenge in developing rechargeable zinc-air batteries is finding a catalyst that can efficiently support the chemical reactions involved in both producing and storing electricity.

During discharge, the battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy. Recharging requires the relevant chemical reactions to proceed in the opposite direction. A suitable catalyst must therefore be effective in both processes.

According to researcher Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero, vitamin B12 "has proven to meet the necessary conditions to act as a good catalyst because, during discharge, it catalyzes the reduction of oxygen to water and, during recharging, it promotes the production of oxygen.".

This ability to support both reactions is what makes the vitamin particularly promising for rechargeable zinc-air battery technology.

Could Vitamin B12 Help Store Renewable Energy?

The successful prototype offers a latest direction for researchers seeking affordable, sustainable alternatives to existing energy storage technologies.

If the approach can be developed further, batteries using vitamin B12 catalysts could eventually help address one of the biggest challenges facing renewable energy: storing excess electricity generated by sources such as solar and wind power for use when production falls.

Industry observers note that although the technology remains at the research stage, demonstrating up to 250 charge and discharge cycles reveals that a familiar biological molecule can play an unexpected role in rechargeable battery design. The discovery adds to growing efforts to use naturally occurring substances to create safer, lighter, and more sustainable ways to store energy.

#86574. Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1011 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gameinformer ↗ Open Full Page

Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gameinformer

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker.
  • In a recent development, void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand.
  • This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker. The ruin is visually spectacular, sure – who doesn’t love to watch buildings crumble because of your grenade or gravity-thrown explosives? But importantly, it’s a critical aspect of Void/Breaker’s roguelite design. Enemies caught beneath falling rubble become instantly staggered, and that’s your moment to kill. Grenades do this too, as do most items you throw at the hostile AI machinery trying to end your run, creating a vortex of shifting priorities as you dash, jump, and shoot at sequential staggered enemies in your sightlines. Countless weapon mods and permutations make fewer than a dozen weapons feel like hundreds in your arsenal, adding even more blissful chaos to the mix. Though it can be difficult at times, if you can see through the literal remains of your destruction, one of the year’s most engaging shooters awaits.

In a recent development, void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand. An AI voice in your head wants your help escaping a simulation where thousands of runners attempt to reach the end of multi-arena stages to defeat a boss. He asks that you simply follow the simulation’s commands; meanwhile, he uses the data you collect along the way to find new exits for you and him. The storytelling style is very reminiscent of Valve’s Portal. Something much larger is at play here, but it’s worth discovering for yourself.

This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure. Mechanically, however, you enter various themed digital stages, from liminal spaces to beaches to snow-capped cliffs and more, and attempt to survive. Most arenas consist of a couple of starkly white structures that your grenades and thrown explosives can topple (ideally onto waves of enemies below). Learning the language of Void/Breaker means constantly scanning your field of view for explosives and structures practically begging to come down, and then eyeing neon-green bars above enemies that tell you they’re staggered and ready for a quick kill. Developer Stubby Games throws plenty of wrenches into this formula, like armored foes and electrostatic enemies you must melee first, and elite bots that will have you on the back foot, but for the most part, Void/Breaker’s formula is “Break stuff, then kill.”.

The game emphasizes explosives and bringing buildings down, but your guns do most of the killing; you can only select one weapon per run. You choose from a pistol, shotgun, machine gun, sniper, and more, and each has its perks (though once I unlocked the SMG, I rarely picked anything else). There’s no sense overthinking your weapon, though, because the dozens of mods you pick up each run determine its effectiveness. As you pick up more schematics, the pool of mods you find in chests or drop from enemies expands, and soon your gun fires corrosive acid, electricity, fire, projectile missiles, and more. Not to mention, mods change how the gun fires, how much damage certain bullets do, recoil, accuracy, and just about any other stat you associate with firing a video game gun. Wild combinations are easy to create, and a unique mod-stacking mechanic that can double or triple effectiveness adds a light touch of puzzle design to this otherwise straight shooter.

Sources indicate that stubby Games smartly emphasizes player expression, never getting in the way of the zanier combinations available to players. The SMG I used to beat the final boss featured mods that made each bullet electric, shot missiles with each shot, covered each bullet in a destructive orb, and featured a ricochet perk that made each bullet bounce off walls and split into even more bullets. I’m thankful for mid-run saves because this SMG permutation, paired with an ability mod that let me throw infinite grenades for a limited time, filled my screen with so much destruction that the entire game crashed. I’d usually bemoan such a thing, but I couldn’t help but laugh. I pushed my PC to its limit with my on-screen chaos.

According to recent reports, boss fights leave a little to be desired – I rarely died because of their simple bullet-hell arenas. Instead, most runs ended because, after bringing down every structure around me, I’d get so lost in the chaos that I wouldn't realize I was stuck in debris while enemies swarmed my location. As stunning as it is to see so much happening on screen, it can be hard to understand what is going on during the most chaotic moments.

Between enemy-filled arenas en route to a stage’s end boss, you might find a shop to buy more mods, ominous obelisks with risk-reward propositions (gain a lot of health or lose half your health, for example), optional trials, and strange phenomena that transport you to different locations. These moments are quick breaks in between bouts of adrenaline-fueled shooter action that I always welcomed – enemies can be relentless, especially as new types are introduced in each stage.

The rest of the Void/Breaker package offers few genre surprises. You can upgrade various traits between runs, research new mod schematics to add to the random pool, purchase new weapons, and discover fun secrets. You can unlock shortcuts, glean in-world information from computer terminals, and hear intriguing dialogue barks from the AI partner who needs your help. It’s all standard stuff for the rogue genre, but if anything, its simplicity pushes you back to the meat and potatoes of this shooter.

It has been revealed that void/Breaker’s shorter runtime – I rolled credits at 12 hours – ensures nothing gets too repetitive in its roguelite structure, but an expansive endgame promises even more to engage with, like different run modifications you can enable to make an already chaotic shooter even more anarchic. I’ll certainly be running it back (again and again) to see what other disruptions I can bring to this AI-simulated adventure. It’s hard not to when destruction feels this good.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Revision 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller revision. When Battlefield Studios announced it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

Industry observers note that the patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

The end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

Recent findings suggest that the other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

And, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the update makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

Read on below for the 1.1.3.5 change log.

GTA 6 had a stellar launch, with two million XBOX players swarming to Fresh Zealand to start their playthrough as early as possible, boasting eye-watering sales figures, and breaking viewership records.

Bugs and glitches are just a part of modern gaming. Some can be game-breaking, others produce some funny moments, and some can actually be useful. One GTA 6 glitch that is gathering a lot of attention is one that lets players access a first-person mode.

As expected, GTA 6 is played in third-person and although many players appreciate a first-person mode, it is absent at launch, or at least, officially.

According to recent reports, there is a glitch that enables a first-person look. It can be a little fiddly at first, but once you get the hang of it, you will have a better view at the sights. We have all the details you need to know about how to enter first-person mode the next time you load up the game.

Industry observers note that youTuber OneBoyler posted a video demonstrating how to do the GTA 6 first-person glitch on PlayStation. To perform the glitch, pause the game and go to the in-game settings, under the Controller tab, scroll down until you see Touch Pad Button. Change the Touch Pad Button to Camera 2. This setting changes your touchpad from opening the map to altering your camera view.

Recent findings suggest that next, sit in the driver’s seat of a vehicle and take out your mobile phone by pressing up on the D-Pad. Put your phone away by hitting circle on a PlayStation controller and then instantly spam your touchpad button.

Recent findings suggest that once successful, you will see the world from your character’s perspective, holding the wheel of the car. From this point onward, you can safely exit the car with first-person view intact and even access your loadout. Equipping a gun allows you to hold it realistically, and the animations are compatible with first-person mode.

Recent findings suggest that bugs and glitches are just a part of modern gaming. Some can be game-breaking, others produce some funny moments, and some can actually be useful.

Also, you can drive in first-person, bringing a upcoming level of immersion to the already gorgeous and detailed world around you. The city lights reflecting off the front of your car hit different when you’re cruising around the streets.

It’s worth noting that to return to third-person mode, you must reload your save. Make sure you save at the right time and don’t make any progress you want to risk losing while experimenting with the first-person view.

Recent findings suggest that when GTA 5 launched on XBOX 360 and PlayStation 3 back in 2013, a first-person mode was absent. Only when GTA 5 was ported to XBOX One, PlayStation 4, and PC did a first-person perspective arrive in the game. Included were an optional first-person cover system, a newly introduced targeting system, traditional FPS controls, and fresh animations that allowed players to see the world in a whole new way.

If history were to repeat itself, a first-person mode could be on the cards for GTA 6 in a future revision. For now, if you want to explore Leonida in first-person, you’ll have to do so using the glitch.

It’s unknown what the first post-launch GTA 6 patch will entail, but if it doesn’t bring a first-person mode with it, players will be hoping that Rockstar Games decides against patching out this particular bug.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nostalgia must be in the air in Maranello. A few months ago, Ferrari unveiled the 12Cilindri Manuale, reintroducing a (simulated) six-speed manual transmission to its model lineup purely for the sake of driver involvement. And now, the Challenge Stradale badge returns to the rear engine mesh of a Prancing Horse for the first time since the 360 CS was discontinued in 2004. Simply put, it's a good year to be a sentimental Ferrarista.

In the same vein as its predecessor, the 296 Challenge Stradale is a road car that shares its fundamental philosophy with the upcoming 296 Challenge Evo racecar, which will debut in the single-marque Ferrari Challenge racing series next year. Parked side by side at their reveal at the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya today, we would excuse a gentleman driver for confusing the CS with his new track-only machinery.

See all results for Ferrari 296 for sale near 29405.

There have been several limited-edition, track-focused mid-engine Ferraris since the 360 Challenge Stradale—including the F430 Scuderia, 458 Speciale, and 488 Pista—but the 296 Challenge Stradale goes the furthest of all of them in emulating its racecar counterpart, both aesthetically and mechanically.

In a recent development, while previous track-centric Ferraris have been somewhat demurely styled, the 296 CS puts its aerodynamic elements on full display. The carbon-fiber rear wing, dive planes, adjustable front splitter, and vented hood are essentially a copy-paste job from the Challenge Evo, with concessions made for road legality. Up front, twin vents positioned in the hood just before the windshield channel hot air expelled from two under-hood radiators over the windshield and towards the rear of the car, reducing the aerodynamic variations caused by changing ground clearance.

Other aero features are hidden out of sight. The CS's underbody has been smoothed to better feed the rear diffuser and work with three pairs of vortex generators at the front and two at the rear to generate additional downforce. With all of the aerodynamic elements colluding, the 296 Challenge Stradale makes 1360 pounds of downforce at 155 mph. That's a 72-percent increase over the base 296GTB's peak figure.

Industry observers note that massive changes have been made to the CS's powertrain. You won't find any orange high-voltage wiring snaking around under the glass of its mid-mounted hood like you would in a 296GTB or 296 Speciale, as the 5-kWh battery pack and rear-mounted axial-flux electric motor have been removed entirely. The twin-turbo 3.0-liter V-6 operates unassisted and supposedly sounds better than ever courtesy of a reworked twin-exit exhaust system.

See all results for Ferrari 296 for sale near 29405.

It has been revealed that overall firepower has decreased to 670 horsepower—149 ponies less than the standard 296GTB's. The upside is a notable decrease in mass, with Ferrari claiming that the removal of the plug-in-hybrid componentry played a major role in shedding 328 pounds from the 296GTB's dry weight. A lightened transmission flex plate, driveshaft, and timing cover were also developed to make the CS's powertrain as featherweight as possible. Without an electric motor present to fill in any thrust gaps left by turbo lag, the V-6 has been retuned to increase low-end grunt, although peak torque remains 546 pound-feet delivered at 8250 rpm.

According to recent reports, as to be expected, yanking out an integrated powertrain system comes with some unique challenges that affect more than just the engine itself. For example, Ferrari was forced to enlarge the 296 CS's rear carbon-ceramic brake discs and the ventilation ducts that cool them to compensate for the lack of regenerative braking. The decreased weight in the rear also shifted its weight distribution 1.5 percent to the front, which was addressed with suspension design and geometry changes.

According to recent reports, the CS's newly developed suspension is derived directly from the 296 Challenge Evo and features semi-active dampers and a dual-spring design that improves rebound response. The result is reduced body roll, which helps the performance of the specially developed Pirelli P Zero R tires, measuring 245/35R20 in the front and 305/35R20 in the rear. The 20-inch forged wheels can be ordered in Matte Grigio Corsa, Matte Nero with a diamond-cut finish, or Matte Bianco Fuji.

The 296 Challenge Stradale's cockpit is very similar to the one found in the 296 Speciale. While niceties like climate control and a stereo remain, carbon-fiber door panels and a lack of armrests and storage pockets are a clear indication of the CS's weight-saving mission. For true gluttons for punishment, an even further stripped interior spec is available that removes the trim from the area beneath the seats and the lower section of the carpets beneath the center console, leaving part of the chassis exposed.

Ferrari is adamant that the 296 CS isn't a replacement for the 296 Speciale and will not cannibalize that model's customer base, as the two are intended for different buyers. Besides being geared less towards outright track duty, the 296 Speciale is a part of Ferrari's special series, meaning that customers need to have an "existing relationship" with the brand in order to get an allocation. The 296 Challenge Stradale is a standard range model, meaning anyone can walk into a dealer and order one, existing relationship or not. Ferrari notes that it wants to court fresh Ferrari buyers interested in experiencing the purest driving experience that the prancing horse has to offer, and the 296 CS is the first step in that direction.

U.S. pricing has not been confirmed, but in its home market, the 296 Challenge Stradale costs 291,000 euros, or the equivalent of about $320,000. Stateside deliveries of the new CS are expected to begin sometime in late 2027. As a non-Speciale model, CS production numbers aren’t limited, which presents a unique opportunity to buy a special new Ferrari without already owning one.

Tech Report: Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1062 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have identified a previously unrecognized inherited form of prostate cancer that, although extremely rare, can lead to aggressive disease relatively early in life.
  • Most cancers develop as genetic changes build up in cells over time.
  • Among the most familiar examples are mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have identified a previously unrecognized inherited form of prostate cancer that, although extremely rare, can lead to aggressive disease relatively early in life. The discovery, made by researchers at the University of British Columbia (UBC), could help doctors identify families with a heightened genetic risk and detect cancer before it spreads.

Most cancers develop as genetic changes build up in cells over time. However, approximately 5% to 10% are associated with inherited mutations that can be passed from parents to their children, creating a cancer risk that may extend across generations.

Among the most familiar examples are mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. These inherited changes can substantially raise the likelihood of breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and prostate cancers. Testing for BRCA mutations has reshaped cancer prevention and treatment by allowing people with elevated risks to receive earlier screening and preventive care.

Now, a study published in Cancer Discovery points to another gene, CDK12, as a potentially vital marker of inherited prostate cancer risk. After examining genetic information from more than 4,500 people with aggressive prostate cancer, the researchers discovered five unrelated men with inherited mutations in CDK12. Every one of these men developed metastatic prostate cancer between ages 44 and 62, meaning the cancer had spread beyond the prostate.

In a recent development, "What's striking is that every patient we identified with this inherited mutation had already developed metastatic disease by the time they were diagnosed," remarked senior author Dr. Alexander Wyatt, associate professor of urologic sciences in the UBC faculty of medicine and UBC President's Excellence Chair in Precision Oncology. "The opportunity now is to identify these families earlier and give people the chance to benefit from enhanced screening, when there are still curative treatment options.".

A Hidden Genetic Cause of Aggressive Prostate Cancer.

Sources indicate that the discovery challenges a longstanding assumption about CDK12. Scientists previously believed that harmful changes in this gene developed spontaneously inside cancer cells rather than being inherited from a parent.

To investigate whether the inherited mutations were actually contributing to the disease, the team examined the patients' tumors for a distinctive pattern of genetic damage associated with loss of CDK12 function. This molecular fingerprint helped connect the inherited mutations to the development of their cancers.

Industry observers note that "The tumors provided us with a genetic signature that pointed directly back to CDK12," said lead author Dr. Sofie Tolmeijer, a postdoctoral fellow in the Wyatt lab. "It gave us compelling evidence that these inherited mutations were playing a direct role in causing their cancer.".

The findings emerged from a broad international research effort involving UBC, BC Cancer, the Vancouver Coastal Health Research Institute, and the University of Washington, along with scientists at institutions in Australia, the Netherlands, Spain, and Belgium.

Despite the potentially serious consequences, inherited CDK12 mutations appear to be exceptionally uncommon. The researchers found them in approximately one out of every 1,000 people with aggressive prostate cancer. Even at that low frequency, they estimate that hundreds of families around the world could be affected.

"While this mutation is extremely rare, the discovery could be lifesaving for the families who carry it," said Dr. Tolmeijer. "Finding one person with an inherited mutation gives us the opportunity to identify other family members at risk and help them take action before cancer develops or spreads.".

Genetic Testing Could Help Detect Prostate Cancer Earlier.

One of the most promising implications of the discovery is that doctors may not need to develop entirely latest testing technology to put the findings into practice.

Sources indicate that the researchers recommend including CDK12 in standard genetic testing panels used to assess hereditary prostate cancer risk. These panels examine multiple genes associated with inherited cancer susceptibility, helping identify individuals who may benefit from closer medical monitoring.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, the clinical technology required to detect CDK12 mutations already exists. That could make expanding genetic testing relatively straightforward, potentially reducing the time and expense needed to bring the discovery into routine patient care.

According to recent reports, "One of the most exciting aspects of this discovery is that we already have the technology needed to act on it," said Dr. Wyatt, who is also a senior research scientist at the Vancouver Prostate Centre and senior scientist at BC Cancer. "Adding CDK12 to existing genetic tests is relatively straightforward, which means this discovery could move from the research lab into clinical care much more promptly.".

Could the Same Mutation Increase Ovarian Cancer Risk?

The study also uncovered clues suggesting that inherited CDK12 mutations might be associated with ovarian cancer, although more research is needed to establish whether they increase the risk.

In a recent development, several of the men with inherited CDK12 mutations had relatives with a history of ovarian cancer. The investigators also identified another person who had ovarian cancer and carried an inherited CDK12 mutation. Analysis of that person's tumor revealed the same characteristic genetic signature seen in the prostate cancer cases.

Industry observers note that together, these observations suggest that CDK12 could potentially play a role in hereditary cancer risk beyond the prostate. Further studies will be needed to determine how strongly the mutations are associated with ovarian cancer and whether they should influence screening recommendations.

In a recent development, for families carrying these rare mutations, the potential benefits of identifying their genetic risk could be substantial. Earlier testing may give relatives the opportunity to receive closer surveillance and, if cancer develops, begin treatment before it reaches an advanced stage.

In a recent development, "With the right genetic testing and screening programs, we envision a future where no one who inherits one of these mutations dies from cancer," remarked Dr. Wyatt.

The research received funding from the Prostate Cancer Foundation, Terry Fox Research Institute, Canadian Cancer Society, Canadian Institutes of Health Research, Michael Smith Health Research BC, U.S. National Institutes of Health, BC Cancer Foundation, and other funding partners.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in what has come to feel like the dawn of the final day before Grand Theft Auto VI's release, one thing that Rockstar really don't want people to be aware of is the ongoing legal dispute between the Rockstar Games Workers Union and the studio itself following Rockstar's alleged union busting in firing 31 union members last year. Starting on the 12th through to the 26th, recognition of the union will be voted upon by staff to ensure that workers would be given a say over "topics including pay and bonuses, overtime, redundancies, flexible working arrangements, and generative AI policies.".

If it passes, the vote would also make the union the largest recognised union in the UK games industry, partly thanks to its partnership with the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain. Now, the global labor union SAG-AFTRA have chimed in to endorse the Workers Union, offering solidarity to the members involved and granting important leverage from a global force.

SAG-AFTRA's statement declares that "unionisation is vital for the future of the video game industry", and that "in the face of record layoffs, job instability, hostile work places, and toxic crunch culture, it is now more critical than ever for unions and workers to stand in support of one another." They advocate for fair treatment, especially in the wake of displacement due to corporate mismanagement and genAI, and proudly state that "this is a fight for all workers.".

According to recent reports, their statement closes by saying that "the gaming industry is a commercial juggernaut, and the people that create these amazing works of art deserve fair treatment and the opportunity to improve the terms of their employment with a strong voice at the bargaining table. We honor the courage of our fellow game workers at Rockstar and proudly support their union vote.".

Solidarity with the workers, always. We can only wait and see how the voting process pans out.

#86565. Industry News: NASA pushes Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1237 w)

Industry News: NASA pushes Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1237 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA is pushing the limits of helicopter flight on Mars, testing rotor blades at speeds once considered too risky.
  • During tests conducted in March at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, engineers successfully pushed the tips of experimental Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound without causing them to break apart.
  • "NASA had a great run with the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter, but we are asking these next-generation aircraft to do even more at the Red Planet," said Al Chen, Mars Exploration Program manager at JPL.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA is pushing the limits of helicopter flight on Mars, testing rotor blades at speeds once considered too risky. The faster these blades spin, the more lift they can generate, potentially allowing future aircraft to carry heavier scientific instruments and travel greater distances across the Red Planet.

During tests conducted in March at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, engineers successfully pushed the tips of experimental Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound without causing them to break apart. The experiments took place inside a specialized chamber designed to reproduce the harsh atmospheric conditions on Mars. Results from 137 test runs could help engineers develop a upcoming generation of more powerful aircraft capable of carrying scientific equipment.

"NASA had a great run with the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter, but we are asking these next-generation aircraft to do even more at the Red Planet," said Al Chen, Mars Exploration Program manager at JPL. "That's not an easy ask. While everything about Mars is hard, flying there is just about the hardest thing you can do. That's because its atmosphere is so incredibly thin that it is hard to generate lift, and yet Mars has significant gravity.".

Recent findings suggest that ingenuity made history on April 19, 2021, when it became the first aircraft to achieve powered, controlled flight on another world. However, it was designed primarily to demonstrate that flight on Mars was possible, not to transport scientific instruments. NASA now hopes to go much further. Its recently revealed SkyFall project, along with other potential future aircraft, could carry sensors and scientific instruments to investigate Mars from the air. Flying at low altitudes would provide valuable information to support future robotic and human missions.

Why Flying on Mars Requires Extreme Rotor Speeds.

In a recent development, helicopters generate more thrust by spinning their rotors faster or using blades with a larger diameter. That basic principle applies on Earth and Mars, but the Red Planet presents a much greater engineering challenge.

Mars has an atmosphere only about 1% as dense as Earth's, leaving helicopter blades with far fewer air molecules to push against. To produce enough lift, engineers must operate rotors at exceptionally high speeds, bringing their tips close to the speed of sound. Small rotors on Earth can also spin thousands of times per minute, but the denser atmosphere makes it unnecessary to push their tips toward supersonic speeds to generate substantial lift.

Recent findings suggest that during Ingenuity's 72 flights on Mars, its engineers limited the helicopter's composite-skinned foam rotors to 2,700 revolutions per minute. This restriction served two crucial purposes. It kept the blades away from the complex and potentially unpredictable conditions near the sound barrier, and it provided a safety margin in case sudden winds (from a dust devil, for instance) caused the blade tips to move faster relative to the surrounding air.

"If Chuck Yeager were here, he'd tell you things can get squirrely around Mach 1," said JPL's Jaakko Karras, the rotor test lead. "With that in mind, we planned Ingenuity's flights to keep the rotor blade tips at Mach 0.7 with no wind so that if we encountered a Martian headwind while in flight, the rotor tips wouldn't go supersonic. But we want more performance from our next-gen Mars aircraft. We needed to know that our rotors could go faster safely.".

Recent findings suggest that the speed of sound also differs considerably between the two planets. At sea level on Earth, Mach 1 is approximately 760 mph (1,223 kph). On Mars, sound travels at roughly 540 mph (869 kph), largely because the atmosphere is much colder and consists primarily of carbon dioxide.

NASA Tests Supersonic Rotors in a Mars Simulation Chamber.

To determine whether the new blades could safely reach these extreme speeds, Karras and his colleagues used JPL's historic 25-Foot Space Simulator. The rotor systems were developed and manufactured by AeroVironment in Simi Valley, California.

Industry observers note that the researchers began with a three-bladed rotor designed for potential future Mars helicopters. After installing it inside the chamber, they removed the surrounding air and introduced a carefully controlled amount of carbon dioxide to recreate the thin Martian atmosphere. They then spun the rotor at progressively higher speeds while exposing it to simulated winds.

Because the experiment involved the possibility of a rotor breaking apart at supersonic speeds, engineers reinforced part of the chamber with sheet metal. The team monitored the experiment from a control room located just a few yards away, using instruments and a camera to track the rotor's performance.

The rotor eventually reached 3,750 revolutions per minute, bringing its blade tips to Mach 0.98, just below the speed of sound. Engineers then switched on a fan to produce headwinds against the spinning blades. With each successive test, they increased the wind speed to push the system further.

Breaking the Sound Barrier Boosts Lift by 30%.

Recent findings suggest that the experiments ultimately drove the rotor tips to Mach 1.08, surpassing the sound barrier and increasing the aircraft's lift capability by 30%. Crucially, the blades survived the supersonic conditions.

Sources indicate that that additional lift could make a major difference for future missions. More powerful Mars helicopters could transport heavier scientific instruments, advanced sensors, and larger batteries, allowing them to conduct more ambitious investigations and remain airborne for longer periods.

It has been revealed that following the successful tests of the three-bladed design, the team evaluated a second rotor intended for SkyFall. This version has two blades that are slightly longer than those used in the first configuration. Because of their greater length, the blade tips could reach the same near-supersonic speed at a lower rotational rate of 3,570 revolutions per minute before simulated headwinds were introduced.

"The successful testing of these rotors was a major step toward proving the feasibility of flight in more demanding environments, which is key for next-gen vehicles," stated Shannah Withrow-Maser, an aerodynamicist from NASA's Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley and member of the test team. "We thought we'd be lucky to hit Mach 1.05, and we reached Mach 1.08 on our last runs. We're still digging into the data, and there may be even more thrust on the table. These next-gen helicopters are going to be amazing.".

Next-Generation Mars Helicopters Could Launch in 2028.

Industry observers note that engineers working on SkyFall have already incorporated the upcoming test results into the project's performance specifications. The findings provide an crucial foundation for designing helicopters that can operate under more demanding conditions while carrying substantially more equipment than Ingenuity.

Inspired by the historic success of Ingenuity, which remains the only rotorcraft ever to fly on another planet, SkyFall is designed to transport three next-generation helicopters to Mars in December 2028.

If successfully developed and deployed, these aircraft could expand the possibilities for exploring Mars, providing scientists with a newly introduced way to investigate the planet's surface and gather information from locations that may be difficult for traditional rovers to reach.

Materials provided by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

In a press release coinciding with Grand Theft Auto VI becoming available for pre-load ahead of its November 19th release date, Rockstar has confirmed that the game "has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits." Read between the lines, and you can kind of make out the words "...so hope your PCs are up to spec, computer nerds.".

Sources indicate that GTA 6, of course, still does not have a confirmed PC version, even if Rockstar's former tech director says it's probably not far off. And despite this, even ancient, last-gen consoles are getting in on it, as the release also unexpectedly confirms that the game will be playable on Xbox One via Xbox Cloud Gaming, Microsoft's game streaming service that has suddenly lost its ability to work on PC. Granted, this comes with a warning: "as with all cloud streaming, connection speeds and other technical factors may influence game performance in ways that would not impact local gameplay." If you ended up getting a PS4 last generation, no cloud play for you either, I'm afraid. It also states that it will "play best on Playstation 5 consoles", making great use of that Sony partnership, and will include Playstation Spectral Super Resolution and ray-traced shadows on PS5 Pro.

A 2026 current-gen game targeting 30fps, let alone one as titanic of a release as GTA VI, is probably not going to go down well with a lot of people, even if console players are traditionally les sensitive about FPS counts than PC players. What this does imply, though, is that the inevitable PC release might be an even more demanding behemoth than expected, if Xbox Series and PS5 versions can't even target 60fps. The availability of the game on Xbox One, even if just through cloud streaming, could have resulted in an acceptance that 60fps just wasn't going to be possible if it was also going to be able to 'run' on last-gen hardware. Either way, when it does eventually escape console exclusivity, hopefully trying to run GTA VI on anything less than an RTX 5080 won't set your PC on fire. Now, let me just promptly have a glance at GPU prices. Oh, no.

In a recent development, as another addition to the slew of smaller studios being dissolved by their parent companies, Bandai Namco unveiled in a press release that they are shutting down their subsidiary studio Reflector Entertainment, a Montreal studio responsible for 2024's action-adventure game Unknown 9: Awakening. In its notice, Bandai Namco explains that the reason for the liquidation is due to Reflector not meeting its expectations for "future business plans, necessary additional investment, and the possibility of profitability and business continuation.".

According to recent reports, the press release notes that the liquidation of Reflector will result in an estimated "extraordinary loss" of around 21 million euros, or 3.5 billion yen, for Bandai Namco in its Q3 fiscal report of this year. This is not the first time Reflector has been cut by Bandai, as around a month after the launch of Unknown 9: Awakening and presumably in response to its low sales, 18% of the workforce was laid off. 2025 then saw further redundancies amidst the cancellation of a prospective project, though details on those layoffs were not granted by the firm. Unknown 9 was intended to be a transmedia franchise involving the game as well as comic books and novels, but these ambitions never came to pass.

Sources indicate that bandai Namco notes that the liquidation will be held to local laws and procedures, which make the actual schedule of the process uncertain for now. A similar process faces Arkane Lyon, which is currently in a purgatory of having been chosen for closure by Microsoft, but temporarily protected by French labor laws that prevent it from being suddenly closed without proper negotiation and procedure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A substantial part of what’s giving Grand Theft Auto 6 its incredible hypnotic power over a statistically-significant portion of the gaming public is its gigantic, intricately-designed world. There are so, so many details to uncover all over the place if you take a moment to stop and look for them, and I’m not just talking about Bigfoot hanging out in the swamps or the many varieties of bird flying around. There are lots of little details that subtly inform aspects of the characters’ personalities and interests, including, apparently, the particular brands of power tools they prefer.

Industry observers note that early in the game, after receiving word that one of the game’s protagonists, Lucia, is coming back from prison, our other lead, Jason, can work to fix up their bungalow home in order to preemptively improve his relationship level with her. This means undertaking a few assorted tasks like repainting and fixing the walls, re-shingling the roof, fixing the stairs, and so-forth.

According to recent reports, A certain subset of players couldn’t help but notice that the tools Jason uses when fixing the walls and roof are colored a distinct shade of yellow. The brand printed on the tool may be different from real-life, but fans of hardware know the distinct iconography of DeWalt when they see it.

For those with no interest in power tools, DeWalt is one of the most prominent brands in the scene, manufacturing all of the usual implements like power drills, nail guns, circular saws, and all that other good stuff, usually powered by rechargeable battery packs. As is so often the case with this sort of thing, fans of DeWalt have something of an unofficial rivalry with fans of other major hardware brands, especially Milwaukee, whose tools are usually colored red.

Recent findings suggest that during Jason’s various household repair chores, he uses a couple of power tools colored the same shade of yellow as DeWalt’s, both emblazoned with the logo “DEVICE.” Obviously, Rockstar can’t just use DeWalt’s actual logo in its game without its permission (though I have a feeling DeWalt would’ve loved it if given the opportunity), but the particular font that the “DEVICE” logo is printed in, particularly with the slightly smaller “E” before the “V,” is unmistakable. Looks like Jason is a DeWalt man, and fans on the DeWalt subreddit are holding this up as a victory over the likes of Milwaukee.

The particular font that the “DEVICE” logo is printed in, particularly with the slightly smaller “E” before the “V,” is unmistakable.

The particular implements that Jason uses seem to be at least partially inspired by real-life DeWalt tools. The driver he uses when fixing the walls is nearly identical to DeWalt’s 20V MAX 1/4 inch impact driver. The nail gun he uses to fix the fencing and roof doesn’t seem to have as close of a parallel, but it most closely-resembles the DeWalt 20V MAX XR brad nailer. That’s not a roofing-specific nailer, though, so either I’m wrong or Jason just doesn’t differentiate between nailer types. I’d believe either scenario.

While this may seem like a granular detail to hyperfixate on, as I mentioned, it’s just kind of fun to examine every aspect of this simulated world. In addition to what I said before about a character’s hardware preferences, it’s also interesting to hold up these simulated knock-off brands next to the real world.

Industry observers note that A major part of the long-established aesthetic of the GTA world is riffing on aspects of real life. It’s always been a very exaggerated setting, often exemplifying the absolute worst parts of modern society for both laughs and drama. The fictional state of Leonida is pretty much Florida if it was slightly worse, and the same goes for Vice City and Miami.

GTA has also parodied more than its fair share of real-life brands and corporations over its various entries, usually with much sillier, ruder names. Sprite becomes “Sprunk,” IKEA becomes “KRAPEA,” and Twitter becomes “Bleeter,” which I am sincerely happy did not change its name to “Blex” or something equally stupid since GTA 5.

#86557. Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1575 w)

Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that as temperatures rise, the floating ice shelves that help hold Antarctica's massive ice sheet in place are melting and breaking apart at record rates.
  • Sources indicate that for years, scientists have believed that ice cliffs become unstable once they exceed 100 meters in height, roughly as tall as the Statue of Liberty.
  • Recent findings suggest that but newly introduced research from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) challenges this long-standing assumption.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as temperatures rise, the floating ice shelves that help hold Antarctica's massive ice sheet in place are melting and breaking apart at record rates. As these protective barriers disappear, they expose towering walls of solid ice. Whether these cliffs remain standing or collapse could play a major role in Antarctica's future ice loss and its contribution to rising sea levels worldwide.

Sources indicate that for years, scientists have believed that ice cliffs become unstable once they exceed 100 meters in height, roughly as tall as the Statue of Liberty. According to this theory, a cliff that grows too tall will collapse under its own weight, exposing an even taller wall of ice farther inland. That fresh cliff would then collapse, potentially setting off a chain reaction that causes the ice sheet to retreat rapidly.

Recent findings suggest that but newly introduced research from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) challenges this long-standing assumption. The findings suggest that the fate of an Antarctic ice cliff depends on much more than its height, and that even dramatic collapses do not necessarily lead to an unstoppable retreat.

Published in the journal Science, the study examined satellite observations of more than 15,000 Antarctic ice cliffs collected over four years. Researchers discovered a surprising pattern: When the cliffs collapsed, they sometimes retreated much faster than existing models predicted. Yet rather than continuing to disintegrate, the affected glaciers soon stabilized.

Recent findings suggest that "We found that when the cliffs were retreating, they were doing so faster than what has been modeled, which would mean more ice loss and higher contributions of sea level rise," says study author Caroline Needell, a graduate student in the MIT-WHOI Joint Program. "But because we found that the retreat was short-lived, and all the glaciers eventually stabilized, that would suggest that things won't be so bad. We don't see this runaway effect.".

The study's co-authors are Catherine Walker, an assistant scientist at WHOI, and Jeremy Bassis, an associate professor at the University of Michigan.

Why Scientists Expected Antarctica's Ice Cliffs to Collapse.

Recent findings suggest that the possibility of runaway ice cliff collapse is described by a theory called marine ice cliff instability (MICI). It proposes that when an exposed ice wall reaches a critical height, its own weight makes it structurally unstable. If the cliff falls and reveals an even taller wall behind it, the process could repeat, progressively eating away at the Antarctic ice sheet.

Earlier research investigated this possibility primarily through computer models. Scientists used the physical properties of ice to estimate how enormous frozen cliffs should behave, then compared those calculations with a limited number of observations from Antarctica. These studies suggested that cliffs taller than approximately 100 meters were particularly vulnerable to collapse.

"Predictive ice-sheet models that have been used so far to represent ice cliff instability just take into account cliff height," Needell notes. "That's the only variable that matters. And once the cliff height reaches the critical threshold, usually 100 meters, it should initiate this runaway effect of ice sheet retreat.".

According to recent reports, needell and her colleagues wanted to test those predictions against a much larger collection of real-world measurements. They sought to determine how tall Antarctica's ice cliffs actually become and whether their collapse consistently triggers the destructive chain reactions predicted by existing models.

Satellites Reveal Surprising Ice Cliff Stability.

In a recent development, to investigate, the researchers turned to NASA's Ice, Cloud, and Land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2). This spacecraft repeatedly travels over Earth's polar regions, using a laser-based instrument called an altimeter to measure elevations with great precision. Its observations track the heights of glaciers, ice sheets, and sea ice, as well as ocean levels in and around Antarctica.

The team analyzed measurements gathered between 2019 and 2023, examining more than 15,000 ice cliffs at three-month intervals. Most were far shorter than the height considered dangerous by earlier models. The average cliff stood approximately 30 meters tall, although a small number exceeded the proposed 100-meter instability threshold.

The researchers also searched for characteristics that might explain why some cliffs remained stable while others retreated.

It has been revealed that one notable clue came from the broken ice accumulating in front of the cliffs. Known as mélange, this material consists of a slushy mixture of sea ice and fragments of icebergs. Cliffs that remained relatively stationary tended to have thicker accumulations of mélange, suggesting that the debris could help support the towering ice walls.

"We measured mélange height and found taller cliffs have thicker mélange, which could be a built-in stabilizing effect," Needell explains.

Surrounding seawater provided another possible source of stability. The observations indicated that deeper water can exert greater supporting pressure against an ice cliff, helping counteract the forces that might otherwise cause it to collapse.

Industry observers note that together, these findings suggest that the stability of Antarctica's ice cliffs cannot be predicted by height alone. Conditions in the water surrounding the ice may also determine whether a cliff remains standing.

Antarctica's Tallest Ice Cliffs Collapse, Then Stabilize.

"After we did that global analysis, we thought, ok, let's zoom in on the tallest cliffs and see how they're behaving," Needell claims.

According to recent reports, the researchers selected four locations around Antarctica where satellites had recorded some of the tallest ice cliffs. Each stood approximately 100 meters high, with the tallest reaching 127 meters. The team then reconstructed how these cliffs changed at three-month intervals throughout the four-year study.

The results initially appeared to support the idea that extremely tall cliffs are unstable. These towering walls did collapse, and the glaciers behind them retreated at speeds substantially greater than those anticipated by existing MICI models.

However, the retreat did not continue indefinitely.

"But that retreat was short-lived," Needell notes.

Instead of retreating farther inland in a continuous series of collapses, the glaciers stabilized and eventually advanced outward toward the ocean again.

"It's this rapid retreat, punctuated by periods of stabilization," Needell says. "That was puzzling to us. Then, we thought: We need to look at all the things that affect cliff height.".

The unexpected pattern suggested that some overlooked physical processes were interrupting the collapse before it could develop into a sustained chain reaction.

Hidden Ridges Beneath the Ice Act as Natural Speed Bumps.

To understand what was stopping the retreat, the team examined the shape of the land beneath Antarctica's ice sheet.

According to recent reports, this underlying terrain, known as bed topography, can strongly influence the height and stability of the ice above it. When the ground is relatively flat, the visible slope of the ice more closely reflects the thickness of the ice itself. But when the terrain rises into a ridge or bump, the ice resting on that elevated ground is thinner than its overall surface elevation might suggest.

These buried rises can function like natural speed bumps. By reducing the thickness of the overlying ice, they can make exposed cliffs shorter and less vulnerable to collapse.

When the scientists compared the locations of stabilizing ice cliffs with measurements of Antarctica's underlying terrain, they found that the cliffs frequently stopped retreating where the ground rose beneath them.

It has been revealed that the researchers identified another important process. Taller cliffs tended to "thin out" more rapidly as they collapsed. Rather than remaining towering, unstable walls, they could swiftly shrink into shorter cliffs that were better able to withstand further collapse.

These effects help explain why the researchers observed rapid initial ice loss followed by periods of stability, rather than the continuous retreat anticipated by earlier models.

What the Discovery Means for Future Sea Level Rise.

The findings could help scientists improve predictions of how Antarctica's ice sheet will respond to continued warming.

According to recent reports, although the researchers observed some cliffs collapsing faster than expected, the rapid retreat was temporary in the locations they studied. This challenges the assumption that crossing a particular height threshold inevitably leads to runaway collapse.

Sources indicate that the results do not mean Antarctica's ice sheet is safe from further losses. Instead, they reveal that predicting its future requires accounting for several interacting factors, including the shape of the land beneath the ice, the rate at which ice becomes thinner, the depth of surrounding water, and the stabilizing effects of broken ice.

"Now we know what to look for," Needell indicates. "We really need to know the bed topography, and we need to know the ice thinning rate, in order to get ice cliff instability right, because this value really matters in the context of projecting sea level rise.".

By incorporating these additional processes into ice sheet models, scientists may be able to produce more reliable estimates of Antarctica's future contribution to global sea level rise.

The research received partial support from NASA, the U.S. National Science Foundation, and the DOMINOS project, which is part of the International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it intends to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

Industry observers note that as discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a massive component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

Industry observers note that the first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the upcoming maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios notes the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of substantial maps as Battlefield 6 at the moment is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

It has been revealed that more Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off newly introduced gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

According to recent reports, battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios remarked we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

According to recent reports, there’s even more exciting news for fans of massive maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is presently in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

Recent findings suggest that for context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its issues elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.
